cases.summary: The audit blocked the run because the cdc_places_county delivery (release 2026-10-01) has 40 of 4,910 rows where the confidence interval does not bracket Data_Value. Those rows were quarantined, which is 0.81% of the source and over the 0.5% quarantine budget, so assert_quarantine_within_budget failed. The contract validation passed because it checks each column's type and range on its own, not how the columns relate to each other. Compared with the previous release, the row count and Data_Value are the same, but the Low_Confidence_Limit mean rose and the High_Confidence_Limit mean fell. That fits the limits being swapped or changed in some rows, but I haven't confirmed it. The 2 cms_geo_variation rows with values like '4.5%' in MA_PRTCPTN_RATE are separate. They stayed within budget (0.34%) and only produced a warning. assert_analysis_cohort_is_substantial also fired on the previous published run, so it is unrelated. Nothing from this run reached consumers. The previously published run 20261019T022136Z-bb5f0a is still being served, and it is consistent.

The new CMS Geographic Variation release (2026-10-15) has 4 telehealth columns that were not in the previous accepted release (fixture-2026-05-15): BENES_TELEHEALTH_PCT, TELEHEALTH_EVNTS_PER_1000_BENES, TELEHEALTH_MDCR_PYMT_AMT and TELEHEALTH_MDCR_PYMT_PC. No columns were removed and no renames were detected. The column count went from 246 to 250, and the row count (583) and suppression rate (0.051458) are the same as last time. The contract policy says unknown columns raise a warning, not a block, so the validate step warned and the run went on to publish. Every dbt test passed except assert_analysis_cohort_is_substantial, a warning that also fired on the previous published run, so it is unrelated. This run's output is what consumers see now. The new columns are not in the contract, so I assume nothing downstream reads them yet, but I did not check the transformation code.

The 2026-10-15 cms_geo_variation release breaks a reconciliation rule. For Pennsylvania (state_fips 42) in 2024, the county rows add up to 109.4% of the state row's beneficiary count (BENES_TOTAL_CNT, read in silver as benes_total). The audit only allows 97% to 100.01%. Payments for the same state-year still reconcile exactly (ratio 1). The schema, the 583-row count, the geography codes and the suppression rate are all unchanged. BENES_TOTAL_CNT's mean rose slightly while TOT_MDCR_PYMT_AMT stayed the same, so the beneficiary counts on one or more PA county rows (or the PA state row) changed in this release. The audit blocked the run before publish. Consumers are still served the previous audited run (20261019T021829Z-d5b53d, release fixture-2026-05-15).

In the cms_geo_variation release 2026-10-15, the per-capita payment column TOT_MDCR_PYMT_PC was republished at a different scale. Its values are about 1/12 of the previous release: median 970.12 now versus 11641.5 before, and the minimum is 419.61 versus 5035.34. That looks like a monthly per-beneficiary figure where an annual one used to be. Total payments divided by FFS beneficiaries still gives the annual amount, so the dbt audit assert_per_capita_matches_totals found 553 mismatched rows. Each one is off by a constant factor of about 12 (for example, derived 11728.9 vs published 977.41). The structure didn't change: same 583 rows, same suppression rate. The contract only checks decimal >= 0, so validation passed. Write-audit-publish blocked the candidate, and consumers are still being served the previous run 20261019T021829Z-d5b53d (fixture-2026-05-15). The warning assert_analysis_cohort_is_substantial also fired on the previous published run, so it is not part of this incident.

The new cms_geo_variation release (2026-10-15) has 68 more County rows than the last accepted release (651 vs 583). These 68 extra rows look like copies of existing rows. They reuse geo codes that are already in the file (BENE_GEO_CD still has 139 distinct values), and their measure values are already present too (distinct counts of BENES_TOTAL_CNT, TOT_MDCR_STDZD_PYMT_PC and TOT_MDCR_PYMT_AMT did not change). The only field that differs is BENE_GEO_DESC, which went from 140 to 208 distinct values, an increase of exactly 68. The contract's duplicate check did not catch them because its grain includes BENE_GEO_DESC, so a different description makes each row look unique. The pipeline's silver-layer row routing removes rows with duplicate natural keys, and it sent 68 rows to quarantine (warn_rows_in_quarantine = 68). That is far above the 0.5% error budget (about 3 rows out of 651), so assert_quarantine_within_budget failed and the run was blocked before publishing. Consumers are still being served the previously published run 20261019T021829Z-d5b53d (cms release fixture-2026-05-15). The assert_analysis_cohort_is_substantial warning also fired on the previous published run, so it is unrelated noise.

I traced the block to a new CDC PLACES release (2026-10-01) for cdc_places_county that has 10 more measures than before. Distinct MeasureId values went from 40 to 50, and the row count rose from 4910 to 5970 (+21.6%). That growth tripped the contract's 20% relative-volume gate (volume.change_vs_previous_release). The delivery looks complete, not broken. The schema is unchanged (22 columns, none added or removed) and every column pattern check passes. Age-adjusted and crude rows stay exactly balanced (2985/2985), and the location count holds at 120. All other contract checks passed, including the grain checks. The new measures are not yet covered by the contract baseline or, possibly, the measure dimension. The runbook's 'Adopting a new PLACES release' step asks for a check of whether the measure list changed. The run was blocked before publish, so consumers still see the previous run (release fixture-2025-12-04).

The cms_geo_variation release 2026-10-15 marks suppressed values with the string "<11" where earlier releases used "*". The contract only recognises "*" (suppressed) and "NA" (not applicable) as sentinels. So in numeric columns, every suppressed cell now fails the integer or decimal type rule. That puts 186 of 583 rows (31.9%) in violation against a 0.5% budget, and the run was blocked at the contract stage. This is a change in how suppression is written, not in how much is suppressed. Row counts are the same (583 vs 583) and the non-numeric counts per column match the old "*" counts exactly (BENES_TOTAL_CNT 29 vs 29, BENES_WTH_PTAPTB_CNT 89 vs 89, BENE_AVG_AGE 30 vs 30). The numeric min, median and max are also unchanged. The recorded suppression_rate of 0 for the new release reflects the marker no longer being recognised; it does not mean suppression went down. Because write-audit-publish stopped the run, consumers are still seeing the previously published run 20261019T021829Z-d5b53d (cms release fixture-2026-05-15).

I couldn't identify a single root cause. The dbt step in transform_audit stopped with exit code 137 before any audit test reported a result. Exit 137 normally means the process was force-killed (SIGKILL), for example by an out-of-memory killer, a container limit or the orchestrator. But the dbt log is empty and the step recorded no counts and no failed tests, so nothing shows what killed it. The only other signal is a contract warning: cms_geo_variation has one new column, BENES_ESRD_PCT, added in release 2026-10-15. The platform's design treats new columns as a warning by intent, and the release has only 583 rows, so the new column is unlikely to have killed dbt. Consumers are not affected: the run was blocked and the previous audited run, 20261019T021829Z-d5b53d, is still being served.
cases.abstain_reason: The run stopped because dbt exited with code 137, which usually means the process was force-killed. Nothing recorded explains why: the dbt log is empty, the step recorded no counts and no failed tests, and there are no host, container or orchestrator logs. That leaves out of memory, an external kill, a timeout and resource contention all possible, so I can't confirm a specific infrastructure cause. The one data-side signal, the new column BENES_ESRD_PCT, is a warning the platform expects by design and isn't plausibly tied to the kill.

cases.summary: Run manual__2026-10-19T17:00:00+00:00 failed in the transform step. The error names Patient/pat-003, but the underlying problem is that bundle bundle-39a12464 contains two Patient records with the id pat-003. The first matches the previous release (gender 'female'). The second is an extra copy with conflicting content (gender 'F'). That copy is the only change from the last accepted delivery: Patient records went from 4 to 5 and total rows from 17 to 18, while the other gender counts are unchanged. The 'invalid gender code' error comes from transform rejecting 'F', which is not in {male, female, other, unknown}. The quality-gate rule that ids must be unique per table never ran because it was skipped after transform failed. So the alert describes a symptom of a duplicate, conflicting patient record rather than a change to the gender coding of the whole feed. Consumers were not affected: the load is a transactional full refresh, it did not run, and runtime/clinical_demo.sqlite still serves the 2026-10-18 tables (4 patients, 6 encounters, 7 conditions), which are internally consistent.

The quality gate stopped this run because one Condition in the new FHIR bundle (bundle-9fb75da4) points to Encounter/enc-007. No Encounter with that id exists in the bundle, which only has enc-001 to enc-006. In the previous accepted bundle, that reference was Encounter/enc-004. Nothing else changed: the schema, row counts, resource types and Patient references are all the same. Because of the failure, load and audit never ran. Consumers are still reading the tables from the last successful run (manual__2026-10-18T18:00:00+00:00).

The new bundle (bundle-faec5e7a) writes every reference in the versioned FHIR form '<Type>/<id>/_history/<n>', for example 'Patient/pat-001/_history/2'. The contract only accepts '<Type>/<id>', and the previous release used that form ('Patient/pat-001'). The patients and encounters being referenced are all still in the delivery: the same ids pat-001..004 and enc-001..006, and the same entry and row counts. But the quality gate compares the raw reference to Patient and Encounter ids, so every reference fails to match: 6 Encounter.subject, 7 Condition.subject and 7 Condition.encounter. The gate stopped on the first one, Encounter/enc-001, with 'missing patient'. Nothing is actually missing, so this is a change in reference format, not an orphan reference. The transform gate is documented as enforcing the '<Type>/<id>' rule, yet it passed these values, which suggests the rule is not applied as written. Load and audit did not run. Consumers still get the unchanged tables from the 2026-10-18 run.

incident.headline: [audit] audit failed - candidate not published: assert_county_totals_reconcile_to_state

diagnosis.summary: The 2026-10-15 cms_geo_variation release breaks a reconciliation rule. For Pennsylvania (state_fips 42) in 2024, the county rows add up to 109.4% of the state row's beneficiary count (BENES_TOTAL_CNT, read in silver as benes_total). The audit only allows 97% to 100.01%. Payments for the same state-year still reconcile exactly (ratio 1). The schema, the 583-row count, the geography codes and the suppression rate are all unchanged. BENES_TOTAL_CNT's mean rose slightly while TOT_MDCR_PYMT_AMT stayed the same, so the beneficiary counts on one or more PA county rows (or the PA state row) changed in this release. The audit blocked the run before publish. Consumers are still served the previous audited run (20261019T021829Z-d5b53d, release fixture-2026-05-15).

evidence.claim: The only failing check is the county-to-state reconciliation audit, and it blocked publish.
PA 2024 county beneficiaries add up to 109.4% of the state total, while payments reconcile exactly.
The audit allows county sums between 97% and 100.01% of the state total; a sum above it means rows were duplicated, dropped or corrupted.
evidence.quote: A sum *above* the state total, or far\n-- below it, means rows were duplicated, dropped, or corrupted between landing and silver.

evidence.claim: The BENES_TOTAL_CNT mean changed between releases while the total-payment column did not.
The row count is unchanged, so this is not a truncated delivery or added rows.
No schema change in the delivery.
The release passed the contract and its suppression rate is unchanged, but it was never published.
Consumers still see the previously published run; this run is not served.
The other 13 checks were skipped, not failed, and no other test failed.

diagnosis.summary: The new cms_geo_variation release (2026-10-15) has 68 more County rows than the last accepted release (651 vs 583). These 68 extra rows look like copies of existing rows. They reuse geo codes that are already in the file (BENE_GEO_CD still has 139 distinct values), and their measure values are already present too (distinct counts of BENES_TOTAL_CNT, TOT_MDCR_STDZD_PYMT_PC and TOT_MDCR_PYMT_AMT did not change). The only field that differs is BENE_GEO_DESC, which went from 140 to 208 distinct values, an increase of exactly 68. The contract's duplicate check did not catch them because its grain includes BENE_GEO_DESC, so a different description makes each row look unique. The pipeline's silver-layer row routing removes rows with duplicate natural keys, and it sent 68 rows to quarantine (warn_rows_in_quarantine = 68). That is far above the 0.5% error budget (about 3 rows out of 651), so assert_quarantine_within_budget failed and the run was blocked before publishing. Consumers are still being served the previously published run 20261019T021829Z-d5b53d (cms release fixture-2026-05-15). The assert_analysis_cohort_is_substantial warning also fired on the previous published run, so it is unrelated noise.

remediation.description: Look at the 68 quarantined rows and their dq_errors reasons and bronze source_line values. Confirm they are duplicate natural keys (the same BENE_GEO_CD/YEAR/BENE_AGE_LVL as another row, differing only in BENE_GEO_DESC).
Send CMS the evidence (68 extra County rows that repeat existing geo codes and measure values under different BENE_GEO_DESC labels) and ask for a deduplicated delivery.

Think about adding a uniqueness rule on YEAR/BENE_GEO_LVL/BENE_GEO_CD/BENE_AGE_LVL. Because the grain uses BENE_GEO_DESC, a description-only duplicate gets past the contract's duplicate-grain block and is only caught later by the quarantine budget.
Re-run once a corrected delivery has landed. The audit gate should pass, and the new release will then be published.

Are the different BENE_GEO_DESC values just alternate spellings or formats of the same county, or a legitimate geography change (rename, split, CT planning regions) that would mean updating dim_geography or the transformation instead?
Did CMS intend to republish these rows, or is this a mistake in how the file was assembled?

Age-adjusted and crude rows stay exactly balanced (2985/2985), and the location count holds at 120. All other contract checks passed, including the grain checks. The new measures are not yet covered by the contract baseline or, possibly, the measure dimension. The runbook's 'Adopting a new PLACES release' step asks for a check of whether the measure list changed. The run was blocked before publish, so consumers still see the previous run (release fixture-2025-12-04).

evidence.claim: The only failing check is the relative volume gate: the row count grew past the 20% limit compared with the 4910-row baseline.
Apart from that one failure, all contract checks passed, including the grain checks.
The number of distinct measures rose from 40 to 50 in the new release.
The column structure did not change; this is a new release, not a schema break.
Value types stay perfectly paired, which fits added measures rather than duplicate or truncated rows.
The runbook says a new PLACES release needs a check of the measure list and the contract.

Then open a PR that documents the expanded measure list and accepts the one-time volume change. Also update the dbt measure seed or dimension so it covers the new MeasureIds, keeping the CI metadata-consistency tests aligned.
Check that the silver and gold models handle the new MeasureIds, mapping or excluding them as intended, so they don't fail joins to dim_measure or get quarantined.
Re-run with `hcip run` once the contract and model changes are merged, so release 2026-10-01 is validated against the updated contract and goes through the dbt audit before publish.

But the dbt log is empty and the step recorded no counts and no failed tests, so nothing shows what killed it. The only other signal is a contract warning: cms_geo_variation has one new column, BENES_ESRD_PCT, added in release 2026-10-15. The platform's design treats new columns as a warning by intent, and the release has only 583 rows, so the new column is unlikely to have killed dbt. Consumers are not affected: the run was blocked and the previous audited run, 20261019T021829Z-d5b53d, is still being served.

The 'invalid gender code' error comes from transform rejecting 'F', which is not in {male, female, other, unknown}. The quality-gate rule that ids must be unique per table never ran because it was skipped after transform failed. So the alert describes a symptom of a duplicate, conflicting patient record rather than a change to the gender coding of the whole feed. Consumers were not affected: the load is a transactional full refresh, it did not run, and runtime/clinical_demo.sqlite still serves the 2026-10-18 tables (4 patients, 6 encounters, 7 conditions), which are internally consistent.

The delivery has one more Patient than the previous release, and the only new gender value is a single 'F'. The original four values are unchanged.

diagnosis.summary: The new bundle (bundle-faec5e7a) writes every reference in the versioned FHIR form '<Type>/<id>/_history/<n>', for example 'Patient/pat-001/_history/2'. The contract only accepts '<Type>/<id>', and the previous release used that form ('Patient/pat-001'). The patients and encounters being referenced are all still in the delivery: the same ids pat-001..004 and enc-001..006, and the same entry and row counts. But the quality gate compares the raw reference to Patient and Encounter ids, so every reference fails to match: 6 Encounter.subject, 7 Condition.subject and 7 Condition.encounter. The gate stopped on the first one, Encounter/enc-001, with 'missing patient'. Nothing is actually missing, so this is a change in reference format, not an orphan reference. The transform gate is documented as enforcing the '<Type>/<id>' rule, yet it passed these values, which suggests the rule is not applied as written. Load and audit did not run. Consumers still get the unchanged tables from the 2026-10-18 run.

evidence.claim: The quality gate failed on Encounter enc-001, whose subject reference is versioned.
The contract requires references in the form '<Type>/<id>'.
Encounter.subject references now carry a _history suffix and none resolve; the previous release used plain references that all resolved.
Condition.encounter references changed the same way: all 7 are unresolved, against 0 in the previous release.
The referenced patients are all still in the current delivery, so nothing is truly orphaned.
Structure and volume are unchanged: no columns added or removed, same entry count.
This run did not load anything; consumers still see the tables from the last successful run.
Load and audit were skipped because the quality gate failed.

remediation.description: Send the provider the profile evidence and ask them to re-deliver with plain '<Type>/<id>' references, as the contract requires, or to confirm that versioned references are an intended change.

If versioned references are an intended upstream change, strip the trailing '/_history/<n>' when parsing references and record the version separately. At the same time, update the contract to allow that form, and fix the transform gate so it actually rejects malformed references instead of letting them reach the quality gate.
Re-run the DAG once a corrected bundle arrives or the parsing change is deployed, and confirm the quality gate, load and audit all pass.

open_questions: Is the switch to versioned (_history) references an intended upstream change (for example, a new FHIR export setting), or a mistake?
The contract says the transform step enforces '<Type>/<id>' references, but transform passed these values. Is that rule actually implemented?
If versioned references are accepted, should the system check that the referenced version (for example _history/2) matches the version of the resource in the bundle?
